sm: The host, Darren Ligan, opens by describing a confrontation on October 30th at Poland's constitutional tribunal, where rival judges took control, police surrounded the building, and the president cut short a foreign trip. His guest, Paul McCarthy, a European affairs senior research fellow, traces the dispute back to 2015, when a new government refused to seat five judges chosen by its predecessor. He says the latest crisis began when Prime Minister Donald Tusk tried to seat four justices and President Nawrocki refused to swear them in. While the president was abroad, Tusk had his justices take control of the court, barring the chief justice and deputy, with about a thousand riot police on the perimeter. McCarthy calls it a constitutional coup and notes that Polish justices are voted by parliament and sworn in by the president as a real check.

Ligan and McCarthy discuss whether the move bypassed constitutional norms. McCarthy agrees it did, and says Tusk cannot credibly defend the rule of law by bypassing it. He calls the police deployment deliberate, a show of force to take control of a key judicial institution, and says it was outside a peaceful democratic process. He says protests were almost entirely peaceful. He describes the president returning to Warsaw and pushing through the police cordon to demand that the chief justice and his deputy be reinstated, which did not happen. McCarthy adds that even members of Tusk's own party have criticized the move, because it sets a bad precedent if the roles were ever reversed.

The conversation turns to fears that the Supreme Court could be the next battleground. McCarthy explains that this court validates elections, and with major elections expected next fall, control of it would matter greatly, so any move on it should draw a forceful international reaction. He says Poland has a strong presidency with veto power over legislation and judicial nominations, and voters chose Nawrocki as a counterweight to Tusk. McCarthy then argues that Brussels is not neutral, saying it backed Tusk and has long acted against conservative governments such as Law and Justice and Viktor Orban. He calls Poland a test case for national sovereignty in Europe, and an important NATO ally on the front line against Russian aggression.

McCarthy says Poland meets its defense spending commitments and has held a strong line on illegal migration under governments of both sides, which he credits even to Tusk. The two note Poland's strategic position near the narrow gap between Belarus and Russia's Kaliningrad exclave. Asked why Americans should care, McCarthy calls the situation lawfare against conservatives, and points to Poland's restrictive abortion laws and the value of national sovereignty. For what to watch next, he names two proposals: a constitutional reset from a coalition party, the People's Party, which would clear the tribunal and vote again but needs a three-fifths majority, and a no-confidence vote from the opposition leading to a technical government until elections in October 2027. He says Heritage stands ready to help with constructive legal solutions.
